{{Short description|Type of prime number}}
In [[number theory]], a '''cluster prime''' is a [[prime number]] {{mvar|p}} such that every even positive [[integer]] ''k''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;p − 3 can be written as the difference between two prime numbers not exceeding {{mvar|p}} ({{OEIS2C|id=A038134}}). For example, the number [[23 (number)|23]] is a cluster prime because 23 − 3 = 20, and every even integer from 2 to 20, inclusive, is the difference of at least one pair of prime numbers not exceeding 23:

* 5 − 3 = 2
* 7 − 3 = 4
* 11 − 5 = 6
* 11 − 3 = 8
* 13 − 3 = 10
* 17 − 5 = 12
* 17 − 3 = 14
* 19 − 3 = 16
* 23 − 5 = 18
* 23 − 3 = 20

On the other hand, [[149 (number)|149]] is not a cluster prime because 140 < 146, and there is no way to write 140 as the difference of two primes that are less than or equal to 149.

By convention, 2 is not considered to be a cluster prime. The first 23 odd primes (up to 89) are all cluster primes. The first few odd primes that are not cluster primes are

:[[97 (number)|97]], [[127 (number)|127]], [[149 (number)|149]], [[191 (number)|191]], [[211 (number)|211]], [[223 (number)|223]], [[227 (number)|227]], [[229 (number)|229]], ... {{OEIS2C|id=A038133}}

It is not known if there are infinitely many cluster primes.

{{unsolved|mathematics|Are there infinitely many cluster primes?}}

==Properties==
* The [[prime gap]] preceding a cluster prime is always six or less. For any given prime number {{mvar|n}}, let <math>p_n</math> denote the n-th prime number. If <math>{{p_{n} - p_{n - 1}}}</math> ≥ 8, then <math>p_n</math> − 9 cannot be expressed as the difference of two primes not exceeding <math>p_n</math>; thus, <math>p_n</math> is not a cluster prime.
** The converse is not true: the smallest non-cluster prime that is the greater of a pair of gap length six or less is [[227 (number)|227]], a gap of only four between 223 and 227. 229 is the first non-cluster prime that is the greater of a [[twin prime]] pair.
* The set of cluster primes is a [[Large_set_(combinatorics)|small set]]. In 1999, Richard Blecksmith proved that the sum of the [[Multiplicative inverse|reciprocals]] of the cluster primes is finite.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.2307/2589585|jstor=2589585|last1=Blecksmith|first1=Richard|last2=Erdos|first2=Paul|last3=Selfridge|first3=J. L.|title=Cluster Primes|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|year=1999|volume=106|issue=1|pages=43–48}}</ref>
* Blecksmith also proved an explicit [[upper bound]] on C(x), the number of cluster primes less than or equal to x. Specifically, for any positive integer {{mvar|m}}: <math>C(x) < {x \over ln(x)^m}</math> for all [[Eventually (mathematics)|sufficiently large]] x.
** It follows from this that [[almost all]] prime numbers are absent from the set of cluster primes.
